doc.title: Tom Varner interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 13, 2025

chapter: Working in New York and Europe
title: A typical week of work in New York: day jobs, Broadway and clubs
summary: Rowe asks about making a living; Varner describes day jobs, Twyla Tharp on Broadway, the Knitting Factory, lofts and European trips.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: In order to make a living, when you established yourself in New York City and during the best years for you what would a week of work entail?

Good question. For some years, many years, even if it was a good week I might have had to do day jobs, just like two or three days a week. Sometimes not. Sometimes – occasionally I did some kind of Broadway show things but not a lot. I was not in the world of the people that did Broadway shows all the time. There was a couple. I did Twyla Tharpe on Broadway, which was a wonderful – John Simon, the guy that had written and conducted for The Band, that guy, he was doing the music and that was a great experience, but that was not a steady type of thing. And I was not in that world of the studio musicians so much. Occasionally I would do something but not on a regular basis like some of the other folks did, like the king of that world was Marvin Stamm. He was the emperor of that world it seemed like at times. But a lot of that dried up in, more like the ‘90s. ‘80s it was just amazing. So a little bit of that. So for me a good week would be – if we’re skipping ahead now to the ‘90s, or the late-‘80s, I would play at The Knitting Factory, whether it was the old Knitting Factory on Houston or the new one on Leonard Street. I would play in other little clubs with other people’s bands. I would play – I’m trying to think where else. Gallery spaces that would have special concerts. Like, kind of like the loft scene, which I had, as a student that summer of ’76, ’77, I’d go to a lot of those loft concerts which was absolutely wonderful. And through either from that or through making other connections, what for me a lot of that time, a good week would be I would be in Europe. I would be traveling a lot. So I would be meeting people through various connections, going to say Amsterdam and having five, six, seven, eight, nine gigs set up, do them, and come back to New York. And then maybe six months later do it again. Do it again. The other thing that was wonderful was that I – speaking of Sheila Jordan – we both played in the George Gruntz big band.
